column9: If the rate of related or unexpected SAEs grade 3-5 rate is > 50% per patients enrolled (after 100 patients enrolled) an interim safety analysis will be required.
column10: Safety-review triggers are permissive, pooled and not arm-specific
column11: A safety analysis is triggered only if related or unexpected grade 3-5 SAEs exceed 50% of enrolled patients, or if pooled mortality exceeds 25%. The mortality trigger has no stated time window. Pooled thresholds can mask a between-arm harm, and the protocol presumes the control arm carries no risk.  Unblinded DMS/DCC staff perform the safety analysis (p.21). This should be reconciled with the statement that only the statistician/designate knows the codes (p.8).

column9: Minor attrition at 1.7% is expected based on results of the TRIPICU study. To account for possible randomization failures, a conservative 1.7% non-compliance factor was incorporated in the sample size calculation.
column10: Attrition/exclusion inflation (1.7%) inconsistent with observed randomised-not-transfused rate
column11: This finding is distinct from SCI-R001 (inconsistent totals) and SCI-R002 (no justification). The protocol does state its assumptions (18% vs 12%, two-sided α 0.05, power 0.90). Recalculation gives about 1484 participants before inflation, consistent with 1538.  The effect-size assumptions are partly defensible: - The 18% control rate sits at the low end of the 15-39% range reported in the observational cohorts (Gauvin, Karam), which is conservative for power. - The 33% RRR lies between the implied RRRs of about 27% (Gauvin) and about 44% (Karam). It is optimistic only relative to Gauvin, whose OR CI includes 1 (1.39, 0.42-4.61).  The main gap is the inflation factor: - Only 1.7% attrition and 1.7% non-compliance are applied. - Appendix 4 reports 7/91 (7.7%) randomised but not transfused, and such patients are excluded from the analysis set. - The 80% adherence definition also implies crossover dilution.  The effective analysed sample may therefore fall below that needed for 90% power.

column9: Written informed consent will be required prior to randomizing a patient in the ABC PICU Trial. Assent should be obtained from the child according to the REB/IRB requirements at each site.
column10: Consent process for parents/legal guardians of critically ill children under-specified
column11: Written consent before randomisation and site-dependent assent are required, but the process is described only in the passive voice. The protocol does not state: - who obtains consent; - that consent comes from parents/legally authorised representatives (only 'family/patient' is mentioned); - how adequate time and comprehension are ensured under acute time pressure, especially for pre-operative consent in scenario 3 before likely urgent surgery; - how long pre-emptive consent in scenario 1 remains valid if a transfusion is ordered days later, or is never ordered; - how participants are re-consented after amendments that add procedures, e.g. twice-daily CAPD delirium assessments.  Participants are minors (under 16) and critically ill, a vulnerable population.

column9: There is no known benefit to individual patients in this study.
column10: Risk/benefit assessment incomplete for randomised pregnant participants
column11: The protocol states there is no known individual benefit, while hypothesising that aPAP improves fetal growth. The risk statements in Sections 5.5 and 9 attribute risk only to device discomfort (HSM) and psychological effects. They do not weigh the following against the absence of individual benefit: - risks of leaving diagnosed OSA untreated in the control arm; - potential fetal or neonatal risks; - burden of the HSM, ultrasound and follow-up procedures.  The safety monitoring rationale is built on this incomplete risk assessment. This finding complements SCI-L005, which concerns disclosure of OSA results and severity thresholds.

column9: Based on an expected mortality of 80% under a hypothetical situation where bacteraemic patients received no antibiotic treatment
column10: 6% absolute non-inferiority margin is wide and justified with inappropriate historical controls
column11: With 8% control mortality, the 6% margin accepts up to 14% mortality in the oral arm, a relative increase of about 75%. The margin is justified by an assumed 80% untreated mortality taken from 1930s Staphylococcus septicaemia case series (refs 23–24), not Gram-negative bacteraemia. The constancy assumption is therefore unsupported. No clinical or patient-centred rationale for the acceptable mortality loss is given. The 8% event rate is a midpoint of 4.4–13.4%. A standard calculation gives about 676 participants, so 720 appears conservative; showing the method is a transparency point only.

column10: Independence of consent from treating clinicians not ensured; neonatal data and vulnerable-context safeguards not covered
column11: Consent responsibilities are allocated by site: Dr Erenbourg in Sydney (p13) and the site fetal cardiologist elsewhere (p12). Three problems remain.  (a) Page 8 commits that participants are approached 'not by their treating doctor'. However, at the international sites the consenting fetal cardiologist, and in all sites the referring perinatal cardiologist who precedes the approach, may be the woman's treating clinician. This risks undue influence, and the protocol gives no safeguard.  (b) Neonatal conditions are collected up to the infant's discharge (p10). No consent process covering the infant's data is described.  (c) The protocol has no safeguards on the timing or manner of approaching families shortly after a fetal CHD diagnosis. It also has no interpreter or translation procedure for the multilingual sites, and no consent to international transfer of data and images to Australia.

column10: Analysed specimen ('diagnostic specimen') not defined as an eligibility criterion; timing relative to ALK inhibitor and type/quality unspecified
column11: Section 4 states that centres will provide H&E images of 'diagnostic specimens', but this is not an eligibility criterion in Sections 6–7. A diagnostic specimen is not necessarily obtained before the first ALK inhibitor or at advanced-stage diagnosis. It could be an early-stage resection obtained years earlier, or a re-biopsy at recurrence, which would change what the classifier predicts.  The hypothesis concerns prediction at diagnosis, before treatment. Yet the protocol does not specify: - Acceptable specimen types (biopsy vs resection vs cytology cell block). - Primary vs metastatic site. - The time window relative to ALK-inhibitor initiation. - Minimum tumour content. - Slide or scan quality criteria.

column9: NR will be defined as a patient that has progressed or died on an ALK inhibitor treatment
column10: Outcome (responder/non-responder label) ascertainment insufficiently defined
column11: The NR label is 'progressed or died on an ALK inhibitor treatment within the first year'. The protocol does not specify: - How progression is determined from routine records (RECIST vs clinician-documented). - How CNS-only progression is handled. - How patients who stop or switch the ALK inhibitor within the first year for toxicity without progression are classified. - How non-cancer deaths are handled. - Whether imaging intervals differ across centres.  The endpoint is framed as 'development of a classifier' rather than as a measurable variable with metric and timepoint.

column9: will include at the learning phase repeated shuffling of the cases from various centers and different
column10: Risk of centre/batch confounding and optimistic performance; no centre-held-out validation or locked test set
column11: Case mix and scanner/fixation characteristics differ by centre. The protocol relies on random case-level splitting and 'repeated shuffling'. This does not prevent the model from learning site-specific technical signals correlated with outcome, and it does not assess generalisability to new centres.  The protocol does partly mitigate this. Site of tissue analysis and site of scanning are listed as covariates (p.5), and the investigators state they will avoid integrating technical factors into the algorithm. These measures do not replace leave-centre-out validation.  The model may also be modified after the validation cohort and cross-validation is added. There is no statement that the test cohort will be locked and evaluated once on a pre-specified final model (also relevant to SPIRIT-27d).
